questions.stem: State the shape and bond angle of BeCl2.
questions.modelAnswer: Linear, with a bond angle of 180 degrees.

questions.stem: State the shape and bond angle of BCl3.
questions.modelAnswer: Trigonal planar, with bond angles of 120 degrees.

questions.stem: Explain why electron deficiency in BeCl2 and BCl3 does not distort their shapes.
questions.modelAnswer: Shape is set by repulsion among the electron domains present; with no lone pairs competing, the bonding domains alone spread evenly - two to 180, three to 120 - so the missing octet electrons simply never enter the geometry.

questions.stem: A student claims BeCl2 should be bent like water because both have two bonds. Assemble the rebuttal.
questions.modelAnswer: Water's oxygen carries two lone pairs that squeeze its bonds to 104.5-ish geometry; beryllium in BeCl2 has no lone pairs at all, so its two domains spread to the full 180 degree line.

questions.stem: State the shape of NH4+ and the bond type that completes its fourth domain.
questions.modelAnswer: NH4+ is tetrahedral, with nitrogen's pair donated as a dative covalent bond to H+ completing the fourth domain.

questions.stem: Explain why spending the lone pair restores the tetrahedral angle in NH4+.
questions.modelAnswer: A lone pair's dense cloud repels harder than any bond pair, but once donated it becomes an ordinary N-H bonding domain; four equal bonding domains then spread to the standard 109.5 tetrahedral angle.

questions.stem: Trace the angle change from CH4 to NH3 to NH4+ and give the cause at each step.
questions.modelAnswer: 109.5 (four equal bonds) falls to 107 when one bond becomes a lone pair whose stronger repulsion squeezes the rest, then returns to 109.5 when that lone pair is donated to H+ as a dative bond, restoring four equal domains.

questions.stem: Explain why a double bond counts as one region of electron density when predicting shape.
questions.modelAnswer: Shape follows how domains repel around a central atom, and both pairs of a double bond occupy the same region between the same two atoms; the geometry responds to regions, not to individual pairs.

questions.stem: Run the full audit for CO2: total valence electrons, bond assignment and final shape.
questions.modelAnswer: Carbon brings 4 and each oxygen 6, totalling 16; two C=O double bonds take all sixteen into bonding; carbon then carries two regions of density, so CO2 is linear.
